# Carbureted Motorcycle Engine doesn't start when hot

A longitudinal V2 750cc Moto Guzzi that cranks effortlessly cold but refuses to fire once warmed up presents a classic thermal dynamics puzzle. The fact that rolling downhill with the clutch engaged allows the engine to start immediately after warming up is the critical clue here. This behavior effectively rules out catastrophic mechanical failure like a broken timing chain or seized piston, as the physical integrity of the moving parts remains intact; the issue lies entirely in the conditions required for ignition and fuel delivery at operating temperature.

The most common internet diagnosis for this scenario is vapor lock. However, dismissing that theory requires understanding the specific architecture of the Dell'Orto PHBH carburetors installed on this build. These are round-slide, gravity-fed units with integral fuel bowls. While modern fuel injection systems often suffer from heat soak affecting sensors or pump delivery, a gravity-fed bowl contains liquid fuel physically separated from the combustion chamber by the needle valve and jetting system. For vapor lock to prevent starting in this specific configuration, the fuel would need to boil within the bowl itself or create a complete vacuum seal preventing flow, which is highly unlikely unless the ambient temperature is extreme or there is an active heat source directly heating the carburetor body beyond boiling point. Since the engine runs smoothly and idles stably, the fuel delivery path is clearly open and functional.

The mechanical work performed so farâincluding ultrasonic cleaning of the carbs, setting float heights to spec, replacing worn needle valves, and installing new intake rubber bootsâhas been thorough. The switch from a points-based OEM ignition to an electronic magnetic pickup system also appears sound. The compression tests show good cylinder health on both sides, even if one plug appears slightly oily after a short test drive. That oiliness suggests worn piston rings, but it is unlikely to cause a total no-start condition, especially given the strong compression readings and the ability of the single healthy cylinder to fire when rolling.

The diagnostic pivot point must be the fuel-air mixture ratio under thermal load. When an engine runs smoothly on a cold start but dies upon heating, the issue is almost invariably a lean mixture or a failure in the transition from idle speed to running speed. The manual choke system adds another layer of complexity. Engaging the choke when hot does not help because the choke enriches the mixture by restricting air intake; if the engine still won't start with the choke engaged while hot, the problem isn't just "not enough fuel," it's likely that the carburetor is failing to meter the correct amount of fuel for the increased thermal expansion and reduced air density at operating temperature.

Consider the idle circuit specifically. As the engine warms, the thermostatic valve in the float chamber opens to allow more fuel into the main jet area, compensating for the richer mixture needed at higher temperatures. If this valve is stuck closed or if the idle mixture screw is set too lean by default, the engine will run fine cold but starve as soon as the thermal expansion of components changes clearances or air leaks increase slightly. The trade-off in vintage carb setups is often between a rich running condition (to cool the cylinder head) and a lean one (for fuel economy). Running hot often pushes an engine into a lean zone where misfires occur, eventually leading to a no-start.

To resolve this, focus on the idle mixture adjustment rather than assuming fuel starvation. Remove the carburetors and inspect the idle circuit passages for debris that might shift position when heated. Additionally, verify that the air intake boots are not allowing excessive vacuum leaks that become more pronounced as rubber expands with heat. If the engine rolls to start, the ignition timing is correct; the issue is purely mechanical metering of fuel relative to air. Adjust the idle mixture screw on each carburetor incrementally while attempting a hot start to find the sweet spot where the thermal expansion no longer causes a lean-out condition.
